title: Herod's mockery (Luke 23:6–12)
hookLine: Herod wants a show, gets silence, and he and Pilate become friends

cards: Early morning in Jerusalem. Pilate, the Roman governor, has a prisoner he doesn't want. Then someone mentions that the man is from Galilee.
Galilee belongs to Herod Antipas, and Luke says Herod is in Jerusalem in those days. Pilate sees a way out: send him over.
So Jesus is walked across town to a different palace and a different ruler, the son of the Herod from the Christmas story. And this Herod is delighted. He has wanted to meet this man for a long time.
Not to listen. To be entertained.

teach.h: HEROD HOPED TO SEE A SIGN.
teach.b: Only Luke tells this scene, and he says what Herod was after: he hoped to see some sign done by him. A miracle, on demand, for the court. So Herod questions him at length.
And then, in the Douay-Rheims: "But he answered him nothing." Remember who Herod is: the ruler who had John the Baptist beheaded. Earlier in Luke, Jesus calls him that fox.
Now the fox has him in the room, and Jesus won't perform. The chief priests stand nearby shouting accusations. Herod and his soldiers, getting no reaction, turn to mockery.

teach.h: A WHITE GARMENT, A JOKE OF A KING.
teach.b: They treat him with contempt and send him back, the Douay says, "putting on him a white garment." A costume. A joke about a king.
Then a strange, quiet sentence: Herod and Pilate became friends that same day, though before they had been enemies.
Two rulers who couldn't stand each other found common ground in a prisoner they both refused to take seriously. Some readers hear in this silence Isaiah's suffering servant, who opened not his mouth.
It isn't sulking, and it isn't weakness. It's a refusal to turn the holiest things into a party trick for someone who only wants to watch.
Someone often wants a performance from us: the clever comeback, the outrage, the show for the audience. Silence before Herod is a way of saying, I won't play that part.

how: Catholics hear Luke's account of Jesus before Herod in the Passion read on Palm Sunday in the year of Luke, and his silence is sometimes linked in preaching with the suffering servant of Isaiah 53.

games.q: you're Jesus. a ruler who killed John the Baptist wants you to do a miracle for his court. he questions you at length. what do you do?
o: do a small sign, so he'll let you go.
argue your case point by point.
games.why: "But he answered him nothing." Herod gets no show, turns to mockery, and sends him back to Pilate dressed in a white garment.

practice: Think of a place where you put on a show: a meeting where you try to sound clever, a feed where you post for applause, a relative who always gets the version of you they expect.
Picture yourself there, quieter, not cold or sulking, just declining the act, with nothing to prove. If you pray, bring that place to God and ask to be the same person in it.

wordCard.voice: Herod's mockery. A ruler who wanted a miracle for entertainment, got silence, and dressed Jesus up as a joke. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: treating as nothing, with contempt, what Herod did to Jesus (Luke 23:11).

carryVoice: Your line: silence before Herod. And that's week sixty-nine: he wept over the city, mites, do this, diakonon, drops of blood, Malchus, and Herod.
